cases.abstract: DreamBooth personalizes a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model from three to five images so that a specific subject can appear in new, text-specified settings. Pairing a rare-token identifier with the subject's class connects the new identity to existing class knowledge; a prior-preservation loss on class images generated by the original model counteracts collapse of the class onto that identity. We release an evaluation suite of 30 subjects and 25 prompts per subject and introduce a DINO-based subject-fidelity metric. On Stable Diffusion, DreamBooth improves DINO similarity from 0.569 to 0.668 and text-image CLIP similarity from 0.255 to 0.305 relative to Textual Inversion. Improvement on both measures supports identity retention alongside prompt-directed variation, rather than resemblance alone. Majority-vote human preferences favor DreamBooth at 68% for subject fidelity and 81% for prompt fidelity. Imagen ablations show that prior preservation reduces class collapse and increases diversity, but slightly lowers subject fidelity. Qualitative examples extend to artistic renditions, novel viewpoints, and property modifications, although context-appearance entanglement, overfitting, and hallucinated details constrain identity preservation.
cases.notes: Revision connects the class-label/identifier relation to personalization and paired fidelity measures to identity retention plus prompt response (Sections 3.2 and 4.1-4.2). Retained the public evaluation suite and DINO metric as co-contributions. Same-backbone comparisons and majority-vote preferences support the central promise; Imagen's prior-preservation ablation qualifies it with a diversity/fidelity tradeoff (Section 4.3), not an isolated explanation of all gains. Qualitative applications remain distinct from measured improvements, and identity failures remain explicit.

cases.abstract: Toolformer learns tool-use decisions from a language model's prediction loss rather than task-specific supervision. Given a few demonstrations per tool, the model proposes calls and retains them when executed responses improve subsequent token prediction over both no-call and call-only alternatives. Fine-tuning on this augmented text turns the model's own feedback into supervision for tool selection, arguments, and response incorporation. With GPT-J and five text-based APIs, prompted zero-shot evaluation encourages calls during decoding but allows at most one per input. ASDiv accuracy is 40.4%, versus 9.6% after text-only fine-tuning and 14.8% with Toolformer's calls disabled, showing that augmented fine-tuning alone does not account for the tool-enabled gain. Factual completion and temporal results improve; question answering exceeds GPT-J baselines but remains below GPT-3, and translation helps without consistently surpassing unmodified GPT-J. With calls disabled, perplexity matches text-only fine-tuning on both evaluated corpora. A GPT-2 sweep places useful tool use near 775M parameters, except for search; stronger base models can diminish weaker tools' utility. Independent call generation leaves chained and interactive tool use unsupported.
cases.notes: Revision links response-dependent loss filtering to self-supervised tool-use learning (Section 2). The ASDiv disabled-call control distinguishes runtime tool benefits from augmented fine-tuning gains; the text-only control supplies the adaptation comparison (Section 4.2), without isolating filtering as the cause. Retained mixed QA/translation results, conditional perplexity parity, scaling findings, and the noninteractive boundary. ASDiv uses the source's numeric-answer criterion, including its equation exception, not exact match. Perplexity parity applies only against text-only fine-tuning with calls disabled; temporal gains do not uniformly establish calendar use.
